introduction-the-master-nodes.core: The control plane is the cluster's brain: kube-apiserver (the only component talking to etcd, serving the API), etcd (the consistent key-value store of all state), kube-controller-manager (reconciliation loops), kube-scheduler (Pod placement) and cloud-controller-manager (cloud integrations). Worker nodes run kubelet and kube-proxy.

first_principles.problem: Engineers don't know which component to suspect when objects aren't created, scheduled or updated.
truths: One source of truth avoids conflicts.
Components communicate through the API server.

analogy.title: A company's head office
analogy.story: Reception (API server), records room (etcd), managers (controllers), dispatcher (scheduler) and site workers (kubelets).
analogy.breaks: Office staff talk directly; Kubernetes components only coordinate through the API server.

example.title: Creating a Deployment
flow: Scheduler binds Pods; kubelets start them

check.q: Which component is the only one that talks directly to etcd?

the-api-server-the-front-door.core: kube-apiserver serves a RESTful, versioned API for all resources, validates and persists objects in etcd, and provides watch streams so clients and controllers receive changes efficiently. Optimistic concurrency uses resourceVersion, and it's horizontally scalable and stateless, with API Priority and Fairness protecting it from overload.

first_principles.problem: A misbehaving controller floods the API server and slows kubectl for everyone.
truths: All reads and writes go through one API.

analogy.title: A busy library front desk
analogy.story: Every book in or out goes through the desk; regulars subscribe to notifications instead of asking every minute.
analogy.breaks: Desks serve in order; APF classifies and fair-queues requests by priority level.

check.q: How does the API server detect conflicting updates?
check.a: Through resourceVersion; stale updates are rejected with a 409 Conflict.

the-3-gates-of-the-api-server.core: Every request passes three gates: authentication (who are you: certificates, bearer tokens, OIDC, service account tokens), authorisation (may you do this: RBAC, Node, Webhook authorisers) and admission control (should this object be allowed or modified: mutating then validating admission, built-in plugins, webhooks, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with CEL). Only then is the object persisted.

first_principles.problem: A Pod with a privileged container is created even though security policy forbids it.
truths: Identity, permission and policy are separate questions.
derivation: **Validate**: Pod Security Admission, policies (Kyverno, Gatekeeper, CEL).

analogy.title: Airport entry
analogy.story: Passport check (authentication), visa check (authorisation) and customs inspection of your luggage (admission).
analogy.breaks: Customs can't repack your bag; mutating admission can modify objects.

example.title: Request journey
flow: kubectl with OIDC token → authenticated as alice
RBAC: alice can create pods in dev ✓

check.q: In what order does admission control run mutating and validating phases?
check.a: Mutating admission first, then validating admission.

etcd-the-clusters-memory.core: etcd is a distributed, strongly consistent key-value store using Raft consensus. It stores all cluster state, needs a quorum ((n/2)+1) of members to accept writes, supports watches and MVCC revisions, and is sensitive to disk latency. Losing quorum makes the cluster read-only or unavailable, and losing etcd data without backups means losing the cluster.

first_principles.problem: A three-member etcd cluster loses two members and the API server stops accepting changes.
derivation: Monitor **db size, leader changes, fsync latency**.

analogy.title: A committee that needs a majority vote to record decisions
analogy.story: With too few members present, no new decisions can be made.
analogy.breaks: Committees can postpone; Kubernetes stops writing immediately without quorum.

check.q: How many etcd members can fail in a 5-member cluster while keeping quorum?

the-controller-manager-the-state-reconci.core: kube-controller-manager runs many control loops (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Job, Node, EndpointSlice, ServiceAccount, Namespace, garbage collector…). Each watches objects via informers, compares desired and actual state and acts to converge, idempotently and repeatedly. Leader election ensures one active instance.

first_principles.problem: Engineers don't know why deleting a Deployment also removes its Pods, or why stuck namespaces won't terminate.

analogy.title: A thermostat for every object type
analogy.story: Each one constantly checks the temperature and adjusts until it matches the setting.
analogy.breaks: Thermostats control one variable; controllers manage complex object graphs.

example.title: Cascading deletion
flow: GC sees ReplicaSet owned by deleted Deployment

check.q: What mechanism makes deleting a Deployment delete its Pods?
check.a: Owner references processed by the garbage collector controller.

the-scheduler-the-dispatcher.core: kube-scheduler watches for Pods without a nodeName, runs the scheduling framework (PreFilter, Filter, Score, Reserve, Permit, Bind plugins) to pick a node, and writes the binding. It supports multiple profiles and custom schedulers, and its decisions respect resources, affinity, taints, topology spread and priorities.

first_principles.problem: Batch jobs need gang scheduling and a different strategy than web services.
truths: Binding is just an API write.

analogy.title: A dispatcher assigning taxis
analogy.story: Checks which cars can take the fare, scores the best one and sends it.
analogy.breaks: Dispatchers can reassign; once bound, Pods don't move unless evicted.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Batch Pods using schedulerName: bin-packing pack tightly.

code.text:
apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration
profiles:
- schedulerName: bin-packing
  pluginConfig:
  - name: NodeResourcesFit
    args:
      scoringStrategy: {type: MostAllocated}
